title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
summary: How skeletal muscles pull on bones in opposing pairs to create movement, and how exercise and rest make muscles stronger.
poll: Muscles can push bones as well as pull them.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Move your arm up and down. What makes it move? Your muscles do!

Muscles are parts in you that pull. You have over 600 of them. They help you walk and jump.

A muscle joins to a bone by a tendon. A tendon is like a string.

Muscles can only pull. They can not push. So they work in pairs. One muscle pulls to bend your arm. The other one pulls to make it straight.

If you use a muscle a lot, tiny tears can form. Rest and food can fix it. The muscle grows back a bit strong.

If you do not use a muscle, it can get weak. So keep moving each day!

Drink water. Eat good food. Rest well. Move each day. This keeps you strong.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Move your arm up and down, or bend your knee. What makes this happen? Your muscles do the work.

Muscles are stretchy parts in your body that pull. The body has more than 600 muscles. They help you walk, jump, run, chew, and smile.

A muscle joins to a bone by a tendon. A tendon is like a tough string. It links a muscle to a bone, so the muscle can pull the bone.

Muscles have one limit: they can only pull, not push. So muscles work in pairs. One muscle pulls to bend a part, like your elbow. The other muscle pulls to straighten it back.

When you use a muscle a lot, tiny tears can form inside it. After rest and good food, your body fixes these tears. The muscle grows back a little thicker and stronger.

If a muscle is rarely used, it can slowly get weak over time. This is why it helps to keep moving every day.

Drinking enough water, eating good food, getting rest, and staying active all help keep your muscles strong for life.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Move your arm up and down, or bend your knee. What makes these moves happen? Your muscles do the work.

Muscles are stretchy tissue in your body that pull. The body has more than 600 muscles. Together they help you walk, jump, run, chew food, and smile.

A muscle joins to a bone by a tendon. A tendon is like a tough cord. It links a muscle to a bone, so the muscle can pull that bone when it tightens.

Muscles have one limit: they can only pull, and they never push. So muscles almost always work in pairs on opposite sides of a part of your body. One muscle in the pair pulls to bend that part, like your elbow or knee. The other muscle pulls to straighten it back out.

When you use a muscle a lot, such as in sports, tiny tears can form in it. After rest and good food, your body fixes these tears. The muscle grows back a little thicker and stronger than before.

If a muscle is rarely used, it can slowly get weak over time. This is one reason it helps to keep moving every day.

Drinking enough water, eating good food, getting rest, and staying active often all help keep your muscles strong for life.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Move your arm up and down, or bend your knee. What makes this happen? Muscles, bones, and joints work together to do it.

Muscles are stretchy tissue that contract, or tighten, to pull. The body has more than 600 muscles. They help you walk, jump, run, chew food, and smile.

Each muscle is made of many thin fibers bundled together. When your brain sends a signal, these fibers contract at once. The pull of thousands of fibers is strong enough to move a bone.

A muscle joins to a bone by a tendon, a tough cord that links the muscle to the bone. When the muscle contracts, it pulls that bone.

Muscles can only pull, never push. So they almost always work in pairs around a joint, the place where two bones meet and can move. One muscle contracts to bend the joint, like the elbow, while its partner relaxes. Then the partner contracts to straighten it back out.

During exercise, muscles work hard, and tiny tears can form in the muscle tissue. With rest and good food, the body fixes these tears. The fibers grow back a little thicker and stronger.

If a muscle goes unused for a long time, it slowly gets weaker. Regular exercise, good food, water, and rest all help keep muscles strong for life.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Moving an arm up and down, or bending a knee, requires muscles, bones, and joints working together. These three body parts must act as one coordinated system.

Muscles consist of elastic tissue in the body that contracts, or tightens, to produce a pull. The body has more than 600 muscles. They let a person walk, jump, run, chew food, kick a ball, and smile.

Each muscle is made of many thin fibers bundled tightly together. When the brain sends a signal, these fibers contract at almost the same time. The combined pull of thousands of fibers is enough to move a whole bone, even a large one like the thigh bone.

Muscles attach to bones through tough, fibrous cords called tendons. A tendon connects one end of a muscle to a bone, so whenever the muscle contracts, it pulls that bone toward it. Without tendons, a contracting muscle would not move anything at all.

Because muscles can only pull, never push, they almost always work in opposing pairs around a joint, the spot where two bones meet and can move. One muscle in the pair contracts to bend the joint, such as the elbow or knee, while its partner relaxes. The partner then contracts to straighten the joint back out, and the cycle repeats with every movement.

During exercise, muscles work especially hard, and tiny tears often form in the muscle tissue. With enough rest and good food, the body repairs these tears, and the fibers grow back somewhat thicker and stronger. This is one reason athletes rest between hard workouts.

If a muscle stays unused for a long time, it gradually weakens. Regular exercise, good food, enough water, and rest all work together to keep muscles strong throughout a lifetime.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Moving an arm up and down, or bending a knee, requires muscles, bones, and joints working together in a coordinated way. Every simple movement depends on this hidden teamwork.

Muscles consist of elastic tissue in the body that contracts, or tightens, to produce a pull. The body has more than 600 muscles, which let a person walk, jump, run, chew food, throw a ball, and smile.

Each muscle is made of many thin fibers bundled tightly together. When the brain sends an electrical signal, these fibers contract almost at the same time, and the combined pull of thousands of fibers is enough to move an entire bone, even a heavy one such as the hip bone.

Muscles attach to bones through tough, fibrous cords called tendons. A tendon connects one end of a muscle to a bone, so whenever the muscle contracts, it reliably pulls that bone toward it. Without a tendon, the strongest muscle could not move a bone at all.

Because muscles can only pull and never push, they almost always work in opposing pairs around a joint, the exact spot where two bones meet and can move. One muscle in the pair contracts to bend the joint, such as the elbow or knee, while its partner relaxes; the partner then contracts in turn to straighten the joint back out, and this back-and-forth repeats with every movement a person makes.

During vigorous exercise, muscles work especially hard, and tiny tears often form within the muscle tissue. With enough rest and protein-rich food, the body repairs these tears, and the fibers grow back somewhat thicker and stronger than before. This is why athletes plan rest days into their training schedules.

If a particular muscle remains unused for a long period, it gradually weakens. Regular exercise, good food, enough water, and enough rest all work together to keep muscles strong throughout a lifetime.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Raising an arm or bending a knee requires skeletal muscles, bones, and joints working together in a coordinated way, a partnership that most people take entirely for granted.

Skeletal muscles, the muscles used for voluntary movement, are elastic tissue that contracts, or shortens, to produce a pull. The body has more than 600 skeletal muscles, which let a person walk, run, chew food, throw a ball, and smile.

Each muscle is made of many thin, flexible fibers bundled tightly together. When the brain sends a signal along a nerve, these fibers contract almost at the same time, and the pull of thousands of fibers is enough to move a bone, even a large one such as the thigh bone.

Muscles attach to bones by tough cords called tendons, which connect one end of a muscle to a bone, so that when the muscle contracts, it pulls that bone toward it. A torn tendon can keep a muscle from moving a bone properly at all.

Because muscles can only pull, never push, they work in opposing pairs, often called antagonist muscles, around a joint, the spot where two bones meet and can move. When one muscle in an antagonist pair contracts to bend the joint, its partner relaxes and lengthens; the partner then contracts in turn to straighten the joint back out, and this pattern repeats with nearly every movement the body makes.

During exercise, muscle fibers get tiny tears, and the body repairs this tissue during rest, often rebuilding the fibers a bit thicker than before, a process called hypertrophy. Enough protein and sleep support this repair well, which is why athletes build rest into their training plans.

If a muscle stays unused for a long time, it loses mass and strength, a process called atrophy. Regular exercise, good food, water, and rest all keep skeletal muscles strong and flexible for life.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Raising an arm or bending a knee requires skeletal muscles, bones, and joints working together in a coordinated way, a collaboration most people never notice until an injury disrupts it.

Skeletal muscles, the muscles responsible for voluntary movement, consist of elastic tissue that contracts, or shortens, to produce a pulling force. The body contains more than 600 skeletal muscles, which allow a person to walk, run, chew food, throw a ball, and smile. Unlike the involuntary smooth muscle in organs or the cardiac muscle of the heart, skeletal muscle responds to conscious, voluntary control.

Each muscle is composed of many thin, flexible fibers bundled tightly together into bundles wrapped in connective tissue. When the brain sends a signal along a nerve, these fibers contract almost simultaneously, and the combined pull of thousands of fibers proves enough to move an entire bone, even a large one such as the thigh bone.

Muscles attach to bones by tough, fibrous cords called tendons, which connect one end of a muscle to a bone, ensuring that when the muscle contracts, it reliably pulls that bone toward it. A torn tendon can prevent a muscle from moving its bone properly at all.

Because muscles are capable only of pulling, never of pushing, they function in opposing pairs, often called antagonist muscles, arranged around a joint. The biceps and triceps of the upper arm provide a familiar example: when one muscle in this antagonist pair contracts to bend the elbow joint, its partner relaxes and lengthens; the partner then contracts in turn to straighten the joint back out, and this pattern repeats with nearly every movement a person ever makes.

During vigorous exercise, muscle fibers experience tiny tears, and the body repairs this tissue during rest, often rebuilding the fibers slightly thicker than before, a process called hypertrophy that depends heavily on adequate protein and sufficient sleep.

If a muscle remains unused for an extended period, it gradually loses mass and strength, a process called atrophy. Regular exercise, nutritious food, enough water, and sufficient rest all work together to keep skeletal muscles strong and flexible throughout life.

versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
Raising an arm or bending a knee requires skeletal muscles, bones, and joints working together in precise synchrony, a collaboration most people never consciously notice until an injury disrupts it.

Skeletal muscles, the muscles responsible for voluntary movement, consist of elastic tissue distributed throughout the body that contracts, or shortens, in order to generate a pulling force. The body contains more than 600 distinct skeletal muscles, which collectively allow a person to walk, run, chew food, throw a ball, and even smile. Unlike the involuntary smooth muscle found in organs or the cardiac muscle of the heart, skeletal muscle responds directly to conscious, voluntary control.

Each individual muscle is composed of numerous thin, flexible fibers bundled tightly together into larger bundles, which are themselves wrapped in connective tissue. When the brain transmits an electrical signal along a nerve, these fibers contract almost simultaneously, and the combined pulling force generated by thousands of fibers proves more than sufficient to move an entire bone, even a large one such as the thigh bone.

Muscles attach to bones by means of tough, fibrous cords called tendons, which connect one end of a muscle to a bone, ensuring that whenever the muscle contracts, it reliably pulls that particular bone toward it. A torn tendon can prevent a muscle from moving its bone properly at all.

Because muscles are capable only of pulling and never of pushing, they function in opposing pairs, often called antagonist muscles, arranged around a joint. The biceps and triceps of the upper arm provide a familiar example: when one muscle in this antagonist pair contracts to bend the elbow joint, its partner simultaneously relaxes and lengthens; the partner then contracts in turn to straighten the joint back out, and this pattern repeats with nearly every movement a person ever makes.

During vigorous or resistance exercise, muscle fibers experience microscopic tears, and the body responds by repairing this tissue during rest, often rebuilding the fibers slightly thicker than before, a process called hypertrophy that depends heavily on adequate protein intake and sufficient sleep.

Conversely, if a muscle remains largely unused for an extended period, it gradually loses mass and strength, a process called atrophy, illustrating the principle commonly summarized as "use it or lose it." Regular exercise, nutritious food, adequate hydration, and sufficient rest collectively work together to keep skeletal muscles strong and flexible throughout an entire lifetime.

Conversely, if a muscle remains largely unused for an extended period, it gradually loses mass and strength, a process called atrophy, illustrating the principle commonly summarized as "use it or lose it." versions.title: Muscles: How Your Body Moves
versions.text:
The seemingly effortless act of raising an arm or bending a knee conceals a remarkably intricate coordination among skeletal muscles, bones, and joints, a collaboration most people never consciously register until an injury or impairment disrupts it, and one whose fluency depends on years of gradual neuromuscular refinement.

Skeletal muscles, the muscles responsible for deliberate, voluntary movement, consist of elastic tissue distributed throughout the body that contracts, or shortens, in order to generate a pulling force; the human body contains more than 600 distinct skeletal muscles, which collectively enable walking, running, chewing, and even the subtle muscular coordination required for facial expression. Unlike the involuntary smooth muscle lining internal organs or the specialized cardiac muscle of the heart, skeletal muscle alone responds directly to conscious, deliberate control.

Each individual muscle is composed of numerous slender, flexible fibers bundled tightly together into progressively larger bundles, themselves enclosed within connective tissue that transmits force efficiently throughout the structure. When the brain dispatches an electrical signal along a nerve, a transmission completed within mere milliseconds, these fibers contract almost simultaneously, and the combined pulling force generated by thousands of individual fibers proves more than sufficient to displace an entire bone.

Muscles attach to bones by means of exceptionally tough, fibrous cords called tendons, which connect one terminus of a muscle to a bone, ensuring that whenever the muscle contracts, it reliably transmits that pulling force to the bone in question.

Because muscles are mechanically capable only of pulling, never of pushing, they invariably function in opposing pairs, conventionally termed antagonist muscles, arranged symmetrically around a joint, the precise anatomical location where two bones meet and articulate relative to one another. The biceps and triceps of the upper arm furnish a familiar illustration: when one muscle within this antagonist pair contracts to flex the elbow joint, its counterpart simultaneously relaxes and lengthens; that counterpart subsequently contracts in turn to extend the joint fully, thereby reversing the original motion.

During vigorous or resistance-based exercise, individual muscle fibers sustain microscopic tears, and the body responds by methodically repairing this damaged tissue during subsequent periods of rest, frequently rebuilding the fibers marginally thicker than before, a physiological process termed hypertrophy that depends heavily upon adequate dietary protein and sufficient restorative sleep, which explains why serious athletes deliberately interpose rest days between successive bouts of intense training.

Conversely, should a particular muscle remain substantially unused across an extended period, it progressively loses both mass and functional strength, a converse process termed atrophy that vividly illustrates the long-recognized physiological principle commonly summarized as "use it or lose it." Regular physical exercise, nutritionally adequate food, sufficient hydration, and adequate rest collectively and cumulatively sustain skeletal muscles in a strong, flexible condition across an entire lifetime, a lifelong investment whose cumulative value becomes increasingly apparent with advancing age.

Second, eat enough protein-rich food, because your body needs it to repair the tiny tears that form in muscle tissue after hard exercise. Third, rest between workouts, because muscles need time to rebuild before you use the same joint again.

keyWords.example: Gymnasts stretch every day to stay flexible.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: Skeletal muscles pull bones in antagonist pairs and strengthen through exercise.
Only the biceps and triceps are ever capable of true antagonist movement.
Nerves are considerably more essential to movement than muscles themselves.
Hypertrophy happens entirely automatically, regardless of exercise or diet.
questions.why: The article explains how skeletal muscles contract in antagonist pairs and strengthen through exercise, rest, and nutrition.

wrong.B: The biceps and triceps are only one example; many muscle pairs work this way.
wrong.C: Nerves signal muscles, but muscles themselves generate the pulling force.
wrong.D: Hypertrophy depends on adequate exercise, protein, and sleep.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is skeletal muscle unlike?
options: Cardiac and smooth muscle, which function involuntarily
Tendons, which are said to never move at all
Joints, which supposedly contain no tissue
Fibers, which are said to never bundle together
questions.why: The article says skeletal muscle is unlike the involuntary smooth muscle in organs or the cardiac muscle of the heart.

wrong.B: Tendons are not contrasted with skeletal muscle this way.
wrong.C: Joints are not described as containing no tissue.
wrong.D: Fibers do bundle together, according to the article.

questions.stem: What does the article identify as an example of an antagonist pair?
options: The hamstring and the heart
The nerve and the tendon
The biceps and triceps
The skull and the spine
questions.why: The article names the biceps and triceps of the upper arm as a familiar antagonist pair example.

wrong.A: The heart is cardiac muscle, not part of this example.
wrong.B: A nerve and a tendon are not a muscle pair.
wrong.D: The skull and spine are bones, not muscles.

questions.stem: In the article, what does hypertrophy refer to?
options: The gradual weakening of a muscle from disuse
The sudden breaking of a bone during a fall
The electrical signal sent by a nerve to a muscle
The growth and thickening of fibers after exercise
questions.why: The article describes hypertrophy as the process where fibers rebuild slightly thicker after exercise.

wrong.A: Weakening from disuse is called atrophy, the opposite process.
wrong.B: Bone breaking is not discussed in this article.
wrong.C: A nerve signal is a separate idea from hypertrophy.

questions.stem: How does the author structure the explanation after introducing skeletal muscle's basic function?
options: By comparing muscles across several different animal species
By moving through fiber structure, bone attachment, antagonist pairs, and exercise
By telling a single long story about one professional athlete
By arguing throughout that muscles matter less than bones do
questions.why: The article moves through fiber structure, tendon attachment, antagonist pairs, and the effects of exercise and inactivity in order.

wrong.C: There is no story about one athlete.
wrong.D: The article treats muscles and bones as working together, not ranked.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what effect does resistance exercise have on muscle fibers over time?
options: It causes immediate, permanent damage that never heals.
It slowly converts muscle fibers into nerve tissue.
It triggers tiny tears that heal into hypertrophy.
It entirely eliminates the need for antagonist pairs.
questions.why: The article explains that resistance exercise causes microscopic tears that the body repairs into thicker, stronger fibers, a process called hypertrophy.

wrong.A: The body repairs the damage rather than leaving permanent harm.
wrong.B: Muscle fibers do not turn into nerve tissue.
wrong.D: Antagonist pairs are still needed regardless of exercise.

questions.stem: A patient has not been able to move one arm for several months due to injury. Based on the article, what would you expect?
options: The arm's muscles have likely undergone atrophy.
The arm's muscles have undergone hypertrophy from rest.
The arm's tendons have slowly turned into nerves.
The arm's joints have stopped needing muscles entirely.
questions.why: The article says a muscle left unused for an extended period gradually loses mass and strength, a process called atrophy.

wrong.B: Hypertrophy results from exercise, not from rest alone.
wrong.C: Tendons do not turn into nerves.
wrong.D: Joints still need muscles to move once the injury heals.

questions.stem: How do skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle differ, based on the article?
options: Skeletal muscle is involuntary, while cardiac muscle is voluntary.
Both kinds of muscle are controlled in exactly the same way.
Neither type of muscle is ever able to contract.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary; cardiac muscle is involuntary.
questions.why: The article states skeletal muscle responds to conscious, voluntary control, unlike the involuntary cardiac muscle of the heart.

wrong.B: The article contrasts voluntary and involuntary control.
wrong.C: Both muscle types can contract.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how skeletal muscles create movement through antagonist pairs, and how exercise leads to hypertrophy, using specific evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how antagonist muscle pairs work across a joint.
I described how exercise, rest, and protein lead to hypertrophy.
I used at least two key words, such as skeletal, nerve, or flexible.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Skeletal muscles can only pull, so they work in antagonist pairs: when a nerve signal causes one muscle to contract and flex a joint, its partner relaxes, then contracts in turn to extend the joint back out. During resistance exercise, this repeated pulling causes microscopic tears in the muscle fibers, and with enough protein and rest, the body repairs them into thicker, stronger tissue, a process called hypertrophy that keeps skeletal muscles strong and flexible.
